newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Toxic poison threatens 75 pct of Russia - report.
newsitem.headline: Toxic poison threatens 75 pct of Russia - report.

text.p: Dangerous dioxins are poisoning nearly three quarters of Russia and make it one of the most polluted countries on Earth, the international environmental group Greenpeace said on Monday.

"Today, since virtually no measures have been taken against this, Russia is one of the worst places in the world, if not the worst" in dioxin pollution, said Veniamin Khudoley, director of the Russian Academy of Sciences' centre for independent ecological testing.
"Perhaps only the territory of Vietnam, as a result of let's say 'chemical agression', would be more polluted," said Khudoley, co-author of a Greenpeace report released on Monday.
He was referring to the U.S. military's widespread use of Agent Orange used during the Vietnam War.
Dioxins are found in certain bleaching agents and weed killers and are known to cause of wide range of diseases including cancer, skin, liver and kidney ailments and birth defects.

Outdated Russian industrial technology, some of which dates back to the rule of Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin, mean that chemical and other factories pump out dioxins into the air, water and soil. From there, the poisons can end up entering the human body.
"A catastrophe has already taken place," Khudoley said. "Almost three quarters of the territory of Russia is affected by dioxins."

The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 has allowed environmentalists to conduct wider studies of pollution across Russia. Their findings have shown massive health problems even in cities where industrial production has fallen off because of the population's long-term exposure to pollution.

Alexei Kiselyov, the other co-author of Greenpeace's "Poisoned Cities" report, said Dzerzhinsk, a centre of chemical production 330 km (206 miles) from Moscow, wins the prize for the most polluted city in Russia and perhaps the world.
"The ground water concentration of toxic agents is 50 million times higher (than the norm)," he said.
"There is not a single healthy person or child there. The average life span in 50 years," he continued. "Apparently, the federal government, knowing the dangers, is ignoring the problem."
The Greenpeace report also said that Moscow, St. Petersburg and other major cities across Russia were badly affected.
Holding up a bottle of mineral water widely sold in Moscow, Kiselyov said Russia eventually burns many of its consumer products, which releases dioxin poisons.

"Here's a simple example, an ordinary plastic bottle. Unfortunately in Russia there are many such examples: not just bottles but toys, rulers shoes, linoleum...many then are burned in garbage factories," he said.

The Greenpeace authors said the most effective way to deal with the dioxin problem is to improve technology at factories, but they also called for government help as many cash-strapped enterprises are unable to afford pollution measures.
